meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Jefferson: a letter to Nathaniel Macon, 12 January 1819. The famous standalone aphorism is the tail of a longer sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1743–1826 · third President of the United States
answer.sourceLine: Jefferson wrote it to Congressman Nathaniel Macon from Monticello on 12 January 1819. It is not an aphorism he coined for the ages: it is the tail of a long, weary sentence about whether the next generation would turn out any wiser than his own.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Writings of Thomas Jefferson, ed. H. A. Washington, vol. VII, p. 112

source.excerpt: My dependence for a remedy, however, is with the wisdom which grows with time and suffering. Whether the succeeding generation is to be more virtuous than their predecessors, I cannot say; but I am sure they will have more worldly wisdom, and enough, I hope, to know that honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom.
trail: The line sits in the sourced section of Wikiquote’s Thomas Jefferson page ↗, filed under 1819 and credited to a letter to Nathaniel Macon dated 12 January 1819.

We read the letter ourselves in The Writings of Thomas Jefferson, vol. VII ↗ (ed. H. A. Washington; New York: John C. Riker, 1857). The letter opens on p. 111 and the sentence falls on p. 112, immediately after Jefferson’s complaint that there is “no measure of value”.
The same sentence appears at p. 122 of Paul Leicester Ford’s edition, vol. X (1899) ↗, where the letter begins on p. 119 — two independent printings of one letter, matching word for word.

Quote Investigator ↗ reaches the same conclusion and adds the detail no printed edition shows: the Library of Congress manuscript ↗ reads “1st chapter”, which Ford’s transcription expanded to “first”.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator, which examined the manuscript images at the Library of Congress, reports that Jefferson’s pen actually wrote “1st chapter”; the “first” everyone quotes comes from Paul Leicester Ford’s printed transcription of the 1890s.

author.bio: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, served as third President of the United States, and founded the University of Virginia — the three achievements he chose for his own gravestone. He is also one of the most heavily misquoted Americans in history, which makes the letters he really did write, like this one to Nathaniel Macon, worth reading in the original.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Jefferson was 75, half-retired at Monticello and, by his own account in this very letter, reading almost nothing but ancient history — “I read no newspaper now but Ritchie’s, and in that chiefly the advertisments, for they contain the only truths to be relied on in a newspaper.”

What roused him was money. The letter is a small tirade about the collapse of stable value in the post-1815 banking boom — eighteen dollars for a yard of broadcloth that used to cost eighteen shillings — and about “swindlers and shavers” who would close their careers in fraudulent bankruptcy. The famous line is his consolation at the end of that complaint: whatever else the next generation lacks, he hopes it will at least have worked out that honesty comes first.
detailsBody: The aphorism travels as a standalone sentence with a capital H and a full stop. Jefferson wrote it lowercase, as a subordinate clause, at the end of a sentence beginning “Whether the succeeding generation is to be more virtuous than their predecessors, I cannot say…” — a hedge, not a proclamation.

He signs off by apologising for the length: “I have made a great exertion to write you thus much; my antipathy to taking up a pen being so intense that I have never given you a stronger proof… how much I value you.”
context.pull: A line about bank fraud, not a motto about character.
